data.title: Excessive Permissions on Network File Shares
data.summary:
Network file shares granted read or write access to all authenticated users,
exposing sensitive business data and credential material to any account in the
domain.
data.description:
Multiple file shares were configured with share or NTFS permissions granting
access to broad principals such as Everyone, Authenticated Users, or Domain
Users. The content held on these shares included business documentation, system
backups, deployment scripts, and application configuration files.

Access of this type requires no exploitation. An attacker holding any valid domain
account can enumerate available shares and recursively search their contents for
material of interest, an activity that generates ordinary file access events and
is therefore difficult to distinguish from legitimate use.

Where write access was also granted, the exposure extends beyond disclosure. An
attacker able to modify scripts or place files in locations from which they are
later executed obtains code execution in the context of whichever user or
scheduled process runs them, frequently a privileged account.

Permissions of this kind commonly originate as temporary grants made to resolve
an access problem, and remain in place indefinitely because no review process
exists to remove them.
data.impact:
Any authenticated domain user could access sensitive business information without
authorisation. Where credential material was present, this directly enabled
privilege escalation and lateral movement. Where write access was granted, an
attacker could modify executable content and obtain code execution in the context
of other users, including administrative accounts.
data.recommendation:
1. Review share and NTFS permissions across all file servers and remove access
   granted to Everyone, Authenticated Users, and Domain Users.

2. Grant access through purpose-specific security groups aligned to business
   function, applying the principle of least privilege.

3. Ensure share-level and NTFS-level permissions are consistent. The more
   restrictive of the two applies, and misalignment between them frequently
   conceals excessive access from administrative review.

4. Relocate sensitive content that does not belong on general-purpose shares,
   particularly backups, scripts, and configuration files containing credentials,
   to storage with appropriate access control.

5. Implement recurring automated scanning of accessible shares for credential
   patterns and sensitive data, so that material reintroduced after remediation
   is identified promptly.

6. Establish a periodic access review so that permissions granted for temporary
   business needs are revoked when no longer required.
